title: Work queues
summary: Move work off the request when the user does not need the result immediately.

parts.rule: A work queue creates a durable handoff between a producer and workers so the request can finish before background work does. Define when the producer may acknowledge, how workers claim and acknowledge jobs, what delivery guarantee is expected, and how retries end. With common at-least-once delivery, every side effect must tolerate the same job more than once.
parts.why: Email, thumbnail generation, feed fanout, and report creation can be too slow or bursty for a request thread. A queue smooths arrival rate and isolates worker failures, but it introduces delay, duplicate delivery, backlog, and a second durability boundary. “Put it on a queue” is incomplete without those consequences.
parts.example: A user uploads photo 42 and needs the original saved immediately, but can wait for a thumbnail. In one database transaction, the API inserts photo(status=PROCESSING) and an outbox row ThumbnailRequested(job_id=781, photo_id=42). It returns 202 only after that transaction commits. An outbox publisher sends job 781 to the queue and marks the row sent, avoiding the crash gap between “database committed” and “enqueue happened.” A worker claims the job with a 60-second visibility timeout, reads photo 42, writes the thumbnail to deterministic object key thumbnails/42, updates the photo to READY, and acknowledges the job. If it crashes after writing the object but before acknowledgement, the queue delivers job 781 again. Writing the same object key and updating by photo_id makes the retry safe. A transient storage timeout retries with backoff; after 5 failed attempts the job moves to a dead-letter queue and the photo becomes FAILED for support or user retry. Monitor oldest-job age and queue depth, then add workers or apply producer backpressure when lag grows. Password verification remains synchronous because the login response requires the result now. A queue changes when work completes; it does not remove the need to report status.
parts.use: Queue slow or bursty work whose result is not required for the immediate response: media processing, notifications, exports, and fanout. Make enqueue durable, give jobs stable identifiers, design idempotent consumers, and expose pending or failed state to users. Scale workers from backlog and processing capacity, not queue existence alone.
parts.refuse: Keep authorization, inventory confirmation, and other response-critical decisions synchronous unless the product supports a pending result. Do not use fire-and-forget memory calls as a durable queue. Avoid infinite retries and consumers that repeat charges or inserts. If the producer cannot atomically persist intent to publish, address the dual-write gap with an outbox or equivalent design.

body:
Rule. A work queue creates a durable handoff between a producer and workers so the request can finish before background work does. Define when the producer may acknowledge, how workers claim and acknowledge jobs, what delivery guarantee is expected, and how retries end. With common at-least-once delivery, every side effect must tolerate the same job more than once.

Why it matters. Email, thumbnail generation, feed fanout, and report creation can be too slow or bursty for a request thread. A queue smooths arrival rate and isolates worker failures, but it introduces delay, duplicate delivery, backlog, and a second durability boundary. “Put it on a queue” is incomplete without those consequences.

Worked example. A user uploads photo 42 and needs the original saved immediately, but can wait for a thumbnail. In one database transaction, the API inserts photo(status=PROCESSING) and an outbox row ThumbnailRequested(job_id=781, photo_id=42). It returns 202 only after that transaction commits. An outbox publisher sends job 781 to the queue and marks the row sent, avoiding the crash gap between “database committed” and “enqueue happened.” A worker claims the job with a 60-second visibility timeout, reads photo 42, writes the thumbnail to deterministic object key thumbnails/42, updates the photo to READY, and acknowledges the job. If it crashes after writing the object but before acknowledgement, the queue delivers job 781 again. Writing the same object key and updating by photo_id makes the retry safe. A transient storage timeout retries with backoff; after 5 failed attempts the job moves to a dead-letter queue and the photo becomes FAILED for support or user retry. Monitor oldest-job age and queue depth, then add workers or apply producer backpressure when lag grows. Password verification remains synchronous because the login response requires the result now. A queue changes when work completes; it does not remove the need to report status.

[[diagram:queue-workers]]

When to use. Queue slow or bursty work whose result is not required for the immediate response: media processing, notifications, exports, and fanout. Make enqueue durable, give jobs stable identifiers, design idempotent consumers, and expose pending or failed state to users. Scale workers from backlog and processing capacity, not queue existence alone.

When to refuse. Keep authorization, inventory confirmation, and other response-critical decisions synchronous unless the product supports a pending result. Do not use fire-and-forget memory calls as a durable queue. Avoid infinite retries and consumers that repeat charges or inserts. If the producer cannot atomically persist intent to publish, address the dual-write gap with an outbox or equivalent design.
